opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of those beautiful moments where two fields that developed largely independently turn out to be talking about the same thing. If you look at a diffusion model, what you're doing in the forward process is slowly adding noise to data until you end up at something like a Gaussian, an equilibrium distribution. And then the generative part is learning to run that process backwards in time. Now, in physics, stochastic thermodynamics has been studying exactly these kinds of processes for a couple of decades: systems driven out of equilibrium, how much entropy you produce along a trajectory, how forward and reverse paths relate to each other. Results like the Jarzynski equality and Crooks' fluctuation theorem are precisely statements about the ratio of probabilities of forward and backward trajectories.

So when you look at it through that lens, training a diffusion model is really learning a time-reversal of a nonequilibrium physical process. And that's not just a cute analogy, it gives you tools. For instance, there are thermodynamic speed limits, bounds that say how fast you can transform one distribution into another given a certain amount of dissipation. That translates directly into questions we care about in machine learning: how many sampling steps do I really need, what's the optimal noise schedule, what's the most efficient path between noise and data? Optimal transport shows up naturally there too.

And the other direction excites me as well. I've always believed that physics has a lot to give machine learning, but machine learning can also give back to physics. If we can learn these reverse processes very well with neural networks, we may get new ways to compute free energies or to simulate molecular systems, which matters a lot for things like materials and drug discovery.

At a deeper level, I find it fascinating that generation, creating structure out of noise, looks like a process that locally reduces entropy, and there's a cost to that, just as there's a cost to computation in Landauer's sense. So there's this question lurking: is there a real thermodynamics of intelligence, of learning and generating? I don't think we've answered it, but diffusion models give us a very concrete place to start asking it.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, for me it closes a loop that started a long time ago. When Jascha Sohl-Dickstein wrote the original diffusion paper in 2015, the whole motivation came from non-equilibrium thermodynamics. You take a data distribution, you slowly diffuse it into noise, and then you ask: can I learn to run that process backwards? And of course you can't literally run a diffusion backwards for free, there's a second law, so the question becomes what does it cost you. That's where the physics gets interesting.

What excites me is that this isn't just a metaphor. There's a very precise correspondence. The forward process is a Langevin dynamics with a drift and noise, the reverse process is also a stochastic differential equation, and the score function that we learn with a neural network is exactly the term that lets you reverse the arrow of time. In stochastic thermodynamics people have thought for decades about things like entropy production along a trajectory, the Jarzynski equality, Crooks' fluctuation theorem, the relation between the forward and the time-reversed path probabilities. And it turns out those same quantities show up in the diffusion model objective. The KL divergence you minimize in training can be read as an entropy production. So the loss function has a thermodynamic meaning.

And that gives you more than just a nice story. It gives you handles. If you know the entropy production is bounded by how fast you drive the system, then you have a principled reason to ask what is the optimal noise schedule, how many steps do you really need, what is the minimal dissipation path from noise to data. Physicists have worked out optimal protocols for pulling a system between two states with minimal work, and those are essentially questions about sampler efficiency in our language. I find that beautiful, that a hundred-plus years of thinking about heat engines and Brownian motion is suddenly directly applicable to generating images.

There's also a personal angle. I was trained as a physicist, I worked on quantum gravity before I moved into machine learning, and for a long time those were two separate lives. Now they're talking to each other again. And I think more generally, generative modeling is becoming a kind of computational physics, where instead of simulating a system you learn the dynamics that generate the equilibrium distribution. That's a very natural way to think about molecules, about materials, which is the stuff I care about these days. So it's not only that thermodynamics explains diffusion models, it's that diffusion models may become one of our best tools for doing thermodynamics.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that it connects a very practical machine-learning method to a physical picture. In the forward process, you gradually add noise, washing out the structure in the data until you reach a simple distribution. Then you learn a reverse process that builds that structure back up.

From the perspective of stochastic thermodynamics, you’re studying how probability distributions evolve under noisy dynamics, and what happens when you reverse those dynamics. The reverse process needs information about the distribution—the score, essentially the gradient of its log density—and that’s what the neural network learns.

So the connection is more than an analogy. It gives us mathematical tools for thinking about the dynamics, where irreversibility enters, and how we might design better sampling processes. I find that interplay exciting: physics helps us understand a generative model, and the generative model gives us a new way to explore questions about stochastic systems.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that thermodynamics gives us a language for understanding how you can turn something disordered into something structured. In a diffusion model, you gradually destroy the structure in data by adding noise. Then you learn a reverse process that takes noise and produces structure again.

From the perspective of stochastic thermodynamics, you can ask: How irreversible is that process? Where is entropy produced? And how should you design the dynamics to get from one distribution to another efficiently? Those become very concrete questions about how we train and sample from these models.

I find that connection beautiful because physics gives you more than an analogy. It gives you mathematical tools, and potentially principles for designing better generative models.
